title: Silicon Valley Is Already Betting on Jensen Huang’s Second Act After Ouster
snippet: Fresh off his dramatic departure from Nvidia amid a national security scandal, tech leaders are rallying behind Jensen Huang, predicting a swift return for the AI pioneer.
content:
SAN FRANCISCO — Barely 24 hours after Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive of Nvidia, Silicon Valley is already mapping out a grand return for the man largely credited with powering the global artificial intelligence boom.

Huang’s sudden resignation sent shockwaves through both Northern California and Washington, where he had built significant clout as a key tech liaison to President Donald Trump. His departure left an unprecedented leadership vacuum at one of the world's most valuable semiconductor giants, just as national security officials and congressional investigators zero in on his alleged affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

Yet even as lawmakers prepare to question him on Capitol Hill, top tech figures are rallying to his side. Defense contractor founder Palmer Luckey and Perplexity AI CEO Aravind Srinivas swiftly defended the ousted executive, while SpaceX CEO Elon Musk openly floated the prospect of hiring him.

A Second Act in the Making

Industry insiders overwhelmingly view Huang’s downfall as temporary. Armed with a personal fortune estimated at $145 billion, deep-seated industry connections, and an unrivaled track record, many expect him to launch a new high-profile venture rather than join an established public firm burdened by corporate governance constraints.

“It is inevitable, with all of the value that he’s created and his role commonly accepted as the godfather of AI, that he will have a second act,” one senior California tech executive noted, adding that top-tier startups and cloud providers are already eager to collaborate with him despite the surrounding controversy.

The Washington Hurdle

While tech leaders remain forgiving, rebuilding trust in the nation’s capital presents a far stiffer challenge. Huang was a vocal proponent of easing export controls on advanced AI chips to China—a stance now under intense scrutiny following reports of his romantic ties to an alleged spy.

Some political figures have expressed skepticism over the espionage claims. Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.) noted it remains unclear whether the individual was knowingly funneling intelligence to Beijing, while tech venture capitalist David Sacks claimed on social media that the narrative surrounding the scandal is already beginning to crumble.

Still, foreign policy experts warn that restoring credibility on national security issues will take significant effort. All eyes are now on an upcoming House committee hearing, where Huang has agreed to testify—a high-stakes appearance that analysts say could make or break his prospects for a political and professional redemption.
